You should determine for yourself whether or not an item is protected by copyright or in the public domain, and then satisfy any copyright or use restrictions when publishing or distributing materials from our collections." The same page asks automated tools to stay under 10 requests per minute (followed while building this plan) and says links "are not endorsements." The Primary Source Sets' background essays and "Suggestions for Teachers" (shown on each set page in place of the older Teacher's Guide PDFs, whose links now return 404), the Primary Source Analysis Tool, and the "Analyzing ..." teacher's guides are written by Library of Congress staff and carry no copyright notice or outside author (all 27 set pages and all linked tool/guide PDFs checked 2026-11-14), so they are works of the U.S. Government, not subject to copyright under 17 U.S.C. §105. The primary-source items (maps, prints, photographs, manuscripts, newspapers, songs, films, oral histories) each carry their own rights statement on loc.gov and are NOT copied here: this plan uses only short item titles, links, and original steps, questions, and answers. Sets credited to non-staff fellows (Civil War Photographs, Civil War Images, and Civil War Music, each "created by" a Liljenquist Family Fellow) were left out.
attribution: Built from the Library of Congress Primary Source Sets (https://www.loc.gov/classroom-materials/?fa=partof_type:primary+source+set) and the Library's Primary Source Analysis Tool and analysis guides (https://www.loc.gov/programs/teachers/getting-started-with-primary-sources/guides/). The primary-source items themselves are only linked, never copied; each carries its own rights statement on loc.gov. Freerange organized 27 sets into daily lessons with original steps, questions, and answers. The Library of Congress does not endorse Freerange or this lesson plan.
description: A chronological U.S. history course, from Columbus and Jamestown to the Voting Rights Act, built on the Library of Congress's free Primary Source Sets. Each day your child studies two or three real maps, letters, photographs, posters, newspapers, songs, or oral histories on loc.gov, using the Library's Observe, Reflect, Question analysis tool, and then answers a few questions. Siblings can share a lesson, and everything is free online.
includes: 45 lessons in 6 units, in chronological order
Links to 27 Library of Congress Primary Source Sets with background essays and teaching ideas
Two or three hand-picked primary sources linked in every lesson
The Library's Primary Source Analysis Tool and a matching analysis guide for each source type
Observe, Reflect, Question steps, map and timeline work
